Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 101, verses 1–3:

﴿The Striking Calamity!﴾ ﴿What is the Striking Calamity?﴾ ﴿And what will make you know what the Striking Calamity is?﴾

Opening with the word al-qari'a (the Striking Calamity) is an opening that inspires awe, and in it there is an arousing of eagerness to know what is going to be reported.

It is in the nominative case, either as a subject (mubtada') with "What is the Striking Calamity?" as its predicate (khabar), and the verse ends there.

صفحة ٥١٠
The meaning then is: "The Striking Calamity is a great thing, it is." This applies on the basis that the first verse ends with the words "What is the Striking Calamity?"

Or else the first "al-qari'a" stands independently by itself, and it is counted as a verse according to the people of Kufa. Then a predicate (khabar) is to be understood for it, omitted, such as "al-qari'a qaribah" (the Striking Calamity is near), or a verb is to be understood, omitted, such as "ataat al-qari'a" (the Striking Calamity has come). And his saying, "What is the Striking Calamity?", is then a resumption (isti'naf) for the sake of inspiring awe, and it is counted as a second verse according to the people of Kufa. On this reckoning the surah is arranged in rhyming units (fawasil): three at its beginning, three at its end, and two in its middle.

The repetition of the word al-qari'a is an explicit mention in a place where a pronoun would be expected. He turned away from saying "al-qari'a ma hiyah" (the Striking Calamity, what is it), because of what the word al-qari'a contains of awe and alarm. Repeating the subject word served in place of the resumptive pronoun linking the subject to the predicate clause.

Al-qari'a is a descriptive adjective derived from al-qar' (striking), which is the striking of one body against another with force that produces a sound. The striking (al-qar') is used figuratively for the sound that the hearer is affected by, with the effect of fear or admonition. It is said: "qara'a fulanan" (he struck so-and-so), meaning he rebuked and reproached him with a voice of anger. In the first maqama (of al-Hariri): "wa yaqra'u al-asma'a bi-zawajiri wa'zihi" (and he strikes the ears with the admonitions of his preaching).

Al-qari'a is also applied to a great event even if it is not a sound, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieved will not cease to be struck by a calamity for what they have done﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31]. It has been said: the Arabs say, "qara'at al-qawm qari'a" (a calamity struck the people) when a dreadful matter befalls them; but I have not found this in what I have seen of Arabic speech before the Qur'an.

The feminine form of al-qari'a is because it is interpreted as an event (al-hadithah) or an occurrence (al-ka'inah).

And "ma" is interrogative, and the interrogation is used for inspiring awe, by way of the compound figurative metonymy (al-majaz al-mursal al-murakkab), because the terror of a thing necessitates people asking about it.

So "al-qari'a" here is meant as a great event. Most of the exegetes hold that this event is the Gathering (al-hashr), so they made al-qari'a one of the names of the Day of Gathering, like al-qiyama (the Resurrection). It has been said: what is meant by it is the sound of the blast of the trumpet (sayhat al-nafkha fi al-suwar). And from al-Dahhak: al-qari'a is the fire that has the roaring (al-zafir), as if he meant that it is a name of Hell.

صفحة ٥١١
This construction is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Al-haqqah﴾ [al-Haqqah: 1] ﴿What is al-haqqah?﴾ [al-Haqqah: 2] ﴿And what will make you know what al-haqqah is?﴾ [al-Haqqah: 3], and it has already been passed over.

The meaning of ﴿And what will make you know what the Striking Calamity is?﴾ is an increase in the awe of the matter of the Striking Calamity. "Ma" here is interrogative and applies to a person, the implied sense being: "What person has made you know?" It is used to magnify its reality and its terror, because the terror of a matter necessitates a search for knowing it. "Adraka" means "a'lamaka" (informed you).

And ﴿What is the Striking Calamity?﴾ is another interrogation used in its literal sense, i.e., "What has made you know the answer to this question?" The interrogation took the place of the two objects of adraka.

The clause ﴿And what will make you know what the Striking Calamity is?﴾ is conjoined (ʿatf) to the clause ﴿What is the Striking Calamity?﴾.

The address in "adraka" is to an unspecified person, i.e., "And what will make you know, O hearer?"

A parallel to this was passed over at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Al-haqqah﴾ [al-Haqqah: 1] ﴿What is al-haqqah?﴾ [al-Haqqah: 2] ﴿And what will make you know what al-haqqah is?﴾ [al-Haqqah: 3], and part of it was passed over at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Judgement is?﴾ [al-Infitar: 17] in the surah of al-Infitar.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 101, verses 4–5:

﴿On the Day when mankind will be like scattered moths﴾ ﴿and the mountains will be like tufts of wool, fluffed up﴾.

(Yawma) is an adverbial object (maf'ul fihi) in the accusative, governed by a suppressed verb indicated by the description of "al-qari'ah" (the Striking Calamity), since it is in the sense of: "it strikes" (taqra'u). Or it is indicated by the entire discourse, so it is estimated as: "it occurs" (takunu) or "it takes place" (tahsulu), "on the Day when mankind will be like scattered moths."

The clause ﴿On the Day when mankind will be﴾ together with its deleted complement serves as an explanation of the two ambiguities in His saying: ﴿What is the Striking Calamity?﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 3] and His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Striking Calamity is?﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 3].

His saying ﴿On the Day when mankind will be﴾ is not a predicate (khabar) about (al-qari'ah), since the context of the speech is not to specify the day on which the Striking Calamity occurs.

The purpose of this timing is to increase the awe conveyed by the two clauses that follow the word (yawma), which convey terrifying conditions. However, the nature of timing is that it be tied to a known time, and since this condition, whose time is tied to its own time, has an unknown extent, the timing of it becomes a means of arousing expectation about specifying the time of its occurrence, since they used to ask, "When is this promise?" Then its timing by what is unknown to them is another ambiguity, for awe and warning against being taken by surprise. It is presented in the form of timing to arouse curiosity to search for its determination. So when the seeker fails to take precaution for its arrival with that which saves him from its calamities, by which ears were struck in many verses.

Thus this verse contains intense awe by eight means: beginning with the name "the Striking Calamity," which announces a great matter; the interrogative used for awe; the explicit noun in place of the pronoun for the first time; the interrogative about what discloses the reality of the Striking Calamity; directing the address to an unspecified person; the explicit noun in place of the pronoun for the second time; timing by a time whose occurrence is unknown; and defining that time by terrifying conditions.

(Al-Farash) is the young locust when it emerges from its egg from the earth, climbing over one another. This is what is in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They will come forth from the graves as if they were scattered locusts﴾ [al-Qamar: 7]. The term (al-farash) may also be applied to the flying insects that fall into fire at night, but that is another usage, and interpreting the word of the verse here with it is not appropriate.

(Al-mabthuth) means: scattered over the surface of the earth.

The clause ﴿And the mountains will be like tufts of wool, fluffed up﴾ is inserted between the clause ﴿On the Day when mankind will be like scattered moths﴾ and the clause ﴿As for him whose scales are heavy﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 6], etc. This is an interweaving (idmaj) to increase the awe.

The point of resemblance is the great crowding over the surface of the place of gathering.

(Al-'ihn) is wool. It is said that it is specific to dyed red wool, or to wool of various colours, as in the saying of Zuhayr:

"As if the crumbs of wool at every halting place they alighted at were the seeds of al-Fana, unbroken."

Because mountains differ in colour in their stones and vegetation, He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And among the mountains are streaks, white and red, of varying colours﴾ [Fatir: 27].

(Al-manfush) means: whose parts are separated from one another, so that it may be spun or used to stuff mattresses. The point of resemblance is the scattering of the parts, because the mountains will be crumbled by earthquakes and the like, so they will be scattered into parts.

The repetition of the word (takunu) with the conjunction is to indicate the difference between the two occurrences: the first is an occurrence of bringing into being, and the second is an occurrence of dissolution. Both are signs of the passing away of one world and the appearance of another world.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the mountains will be like wool﴾ has already been mentioned in Surat al-Ma'arij.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 101, verses 6–11:**

﴿As for him whose scales are heavy, [6] he will be in a pleasing life.﴾ ﴿But as for him whose scales are light, [8] his mother will be the Abyss. [9] And what can make you know what it is? [10] A blazing Fire. [11]﴾

This elaborates what is stated in His words: ﴿On the Day when people will be like scattered moths﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 4], from the general description of people's condition at that time. That is the purpose of mentioning the word "people," which includes both the people of happiness and the people of misery. For this reason, its elaboration is in two conditions: a good condition and a dreadful condition.

The heaviness of the scales is a kinaya (metonymy) for being in a place of God's good pleasure because of the abundance of one's good deeds, since the heaviness of the scale implies the heaviness of what is weighed. Things are weighed only when they are desired to be possessed. Among the Arabs, it was widespread to use weighing and the like as a kinaya for virtue, nobility and soundness of judgment. In the opposite sense they say, "So-and-so has no weight given to him." God, Exalted, says: ﴿So We shall not assign them any weight on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Kahf: 105]. Al-Nabigha said:

*"And his scale in the realm of glory is weighty."*

That is, it is heavy. This is evident in the Arabic language, so the verse does not explicitly mention what makes the scales heavy, since it is clear that it is righteous deeds.

The mention of the scale for deeds on the Day of Resurrection occurs frequently in the Qur'an. Ibn al-'Arabi said in *al-'Awasim*: "No authentic hadith has been reported about the scale." The purpose is that no deed is lost, and God is able to make that on the Day of Resurrection by means of an instrument, or by the work of the angels, or something of that kind.

[p. 514]

*Al-'Ishah* is a verbal noun of *al-'aysh* (life), like *al-khifah* (fear), which is a noun for fear. That is: in a life.

Describing life as *radiyah* (pleasing) is a rational metaphor (*majaz 'aqli*), because the one who is pleased is its owner who is pleased with it. So *al-'ishah* is described with it because it is the cause of pleasure or the time of pleasure.

His words: ﴿his mother will be the Abyss﴾ are information about his misery and bad condition. The word *umm* (mother) here may be used in its literal sense. *Hawiyah* means "destroyed," and the statement is an image (*tamthil*) of the condition of the one whose scales are light on that day, by the condition of one who is destroyed in this world. This is because the Arabs use the condition of one's mother as a kinaya for a person's condition, good or bad, because of the intensity of her love for her son: she is more joyful at his joy and more sorrowful at what grieves him. A Bedouin prayed behind an imam, and the imam recited ﴿And God took Abraham as a close friend﴾ [al-Nisa': 125]. The Bedouin said: "The eye of Abraham's mother has been cooled!" From this is the saying of Ibn Zayyabah when al-Harith ibn Hammam al-Shaybani threatened him:

*"Alas for Zayyabah, for al-Harith al-Sabih, then al-Ghanim, then al-Ayib."*

In evil they say: "His mother has fallen," meaning: he has been struck by what his mother perishes from. This is like their saying "May his mother be bereft" as an invocation. Some of it is used in expressing amazement, and its origin is supplication, as in the saying of Ka'b ibn Sa'd al-Ghanawi in lamenting his brother Abu al-Mighwar:

*"Woe to his mother, what the morning sends forth at dawn, and what the night returns with at its coming back."*

That is: what the morning sends forth from him at dawn, and what the night returns with when it comes back a victor. The implied *min* (from) is *tajridiyyah* (abstraction), so the statement is in the mode of abstraction, like: "I met from him a lion."

So the compound that is said at the moment of destruction and bad fate is used for a condition likened to the condition of destruction, and it symbolizes the comparison by that compound, just as proverbs are coined.

It is also possible that *ummuhu* (his mother) is a metaphor for his resting place and his end, because he returns to it as a child returns to his mother.

*Hawiyah* is the low place between two mountains, into which if a human or an animal falls, it perishes. It is said: "He fell into the *hawiyah*."

It is meant to be Jahannam. It was also said that it is a name for Jahannam, that is: his refuge is Jahannam.

[p. 515]

It is also possible that *ummuhu* is by omission of a modifier, that is: "the mother of his head," meaning: he perished.

﴿And what can make you know what it is?﴾ is an expression of awe, as mentioned above.

The pronoun in *hiyah* refers to *hawiyah*. So according to the first view, there is an *istikhdam* (a figure in which a pronoun is made to refer to one meaning of a word and then to another) in the pronoun, since the referent of the pronoun is the description "destroyed," while what is intended by it is the name of Jahannam, as in the saying of Mu'awiya ibn Malik, nicknamed Mu'awwidh al-Hukama':

*"When rain falls on the land of a people, we graze it, even if they are angry."*

According to the second view, the pronoun refers to *hawiyah*, and it is interpreted as meaning the bottom of Jahannam.

According to the third view, there is also an *istikhdam* in *hiyah*, as in the first view.

The *ha'* that attaches to the *ya'* of *hiya* is *ha' al-sakt* (the pausal *ha'*). It is a *ha'* added to ease pronunciation when pausing upon the word. Some of this is obligatory, where the *ha'* is necessarily added, and some of it is good but not obligatory. This applies to every noun or particle that ends in a permanent vowel of construction, such as *huwa*, *hiya*, *kayfa*, and *thumma*. This was previously discussed at His words: ﴿As for him who is given his record in his right hand﴾ [al-Haqqah: 19] ﴿he will say, "Here, read my record!"﴾ [al-Haqqah: 19], in surah al-Haqqah.

The majority of the readers (*qurra'*) affirmed the pronunciation of this *ha'* in both pausal and continuous recitation, while Hamzah and Khalaf read with the *ha'* in pause and omitted it in continuous recitation.

The clause ﴿A blazing Fire﴾ is an explanation of the clause ﴿And what can make you know what it is?﴾, and the meaning is: "It is a blazing Fire." This is an omission of the subject (*al-musnad ilayhi*), which the usage of the lexicographers has followed in its omission.

The description of *nar* (Fire) as *hamiyah* (blazing) is a verbal emphasis (*tawkid lafzi*), because the Fire is never free of heat, so describing it with it is describing it with what is the meaning of the word *nar*. It is like mentioning a synonym, as in His words: ﴿the Fire of God, kindled﴾ [al-Humazah: 6].

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

Surah al-Takathur

Al-Alusi said: Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Abi Hilal: "The Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to call it *al-Maqbarah* (the Graveyard)." End of quotation.

It is named in most of the *mushafs* and most of the tafsirs *Surat al-Takathur*, and al-Tirmidhi also titled it so in his *Jami'*. It is also titled so in some ancient *mushafs* in Qayrawan.

It is named in some *mushafs* *Surat Alhakum* (Surah "Alhakum"), and al-Bukhari also titled it so in the Book of Tafsir of his *Sahih*.

It is Meccan according to the majority. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is Meccan; I know of no disagreement about it."

From Ibn 'Abbas, al-Kalbi and Muqatil: it was revealed concerning a boasting that took place between the Banu 'Abd Manaf and the Banu Sahm in Islam, as will come shortly. They were among the clans of Quraysh in Mecca, and the graves of their forebears are in Mecca.

In *al-Itqan*: "The preferred view is that it is Medinan." He said: "What supports this is what Ibn Abi Hatim reported, that it was revealed concerning two tribes of the Ansar who boasted to each other." And what al-Bukhari reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "If the son of Adam had a valley of gold, he would love to have two valleys, and nothing will fill his mouth but dust. God relents toward whoever repents." Ubayy said: "We used to regard this as part of the Qur'an until ﴿Rivalry in worldly increase diverts you﴾ [al-Takathur: 1] was revealed." End of quotation. The one who cites this intends that Ubayy was an Ansari, and that the apparent meaning of his words "until it was revealed" is that it was revealed after they had counted "If the son of Adam had a valley of gold..." as part of the Qur'an. But there is no conclusive evidence in Ubayy's words, since it is possible that by the pronoun in "we" he means the Muslims, that is: whoever preceded them used to count that as Qur'an until the surah of al-Takathur was revealed, and the Prophet (ﷺ) explained to them that what they were saying was not Qur'an.

[p. 518]

What appears from the meanings of the surah and the severity of its warning is that it is Meccan, and that its addressees are a group of the polytheists, because what is mentioned in it is not fitting for the Muslims at that time.

The cause of its revelation, as said by al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi from Muqatil and al-Kalbi, and al-Qurtubi from them both and from Ibn 'Abbas, is that the Banu 'Abd Manaf and the Banu Sahm from Quraysh boasted, so they counted the chiefs and nobles of each to see which of them was more numerous. The Banu 'Abd Manaf outnumbered the Banu Sahm by three clans, because they were more numerous in the pre-Islamic era.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Buraydah al-Jarmi who said: "It was revealed concerning two tribes of the Ansar: the Banu Harithah and the Banu al-Harith. They boasted and vied with each other in their living members, then they said: 'Come, let us go to the graves.' One of the two groups began to say: 'Among you is someone like so-and-so,' pointing to a grave, 'and like so-and-so,' and the others did likewise. So God revealed: ﴿Rivalry in worldly increase diverts you﴾ [al-Takathur: 1]."

It is counted the sixteenth in the order of revelation of the surahs, and it was revealed after Surat al-Kawthar and before Surat al-Ma'un, based on its being Meccan.

The number of its verses is eight.

* * *

It contains a rebuke for being diverted from reflecting on the proofs of the Qur'an and the call of Islam by preferring wealth, competing in it, boasting of ancestors, and not desisting from that until they enter the graves as those before them did, and a warning for that.

It exhorts them to reflect on what will save them from the Blazing Fire (*al-Jahim*).

And that they will be resurrected and held accountable for neglecting to thank the Great Benefactor.
